What Lake Nona Homeowners Should Know Before Installing Turf

Turf in Lake Nona answers to two different governments depending on which side of Narcoossee Road a lot sits, on top of a Tavistock design review that already names artificial turf. As of September 2026, the west side runs Orlando's engineering permit, while a Laureate Park backyard still needs sign-off from the community's own architectural board before a blade goes down.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Which government reviews a turf permit here

Lake Nona sits about 11 miles from downtown Kissimmee, split down the middle by Narcoossee Road. West of that road, Laureate Park, VillageWalk, Lake Nona Golf & Country Club and Northlake Park sit inside the Tavistock-built footprint that the City of Orlando annexed. East of it, Storey Park, Eagle Creek and the streets around Moss Park fall under unincorporated Orange County instead, a line a local guide to the area lays out street by street (boundary guide). A parcel search on the Orange County Property Appraiser confirms a specific address, since the area's two ZIP codes, 32827 and 32832, only roughly track the Narcoossee Road line rather than match it exactly.

That split decides which permit page applies before anything else does. A Laureate Park or Northlake Park address answers to Orlando Permitting Services, the one office in the region with a landscape-code section written for synthetic turf by name. A Storey Park or Eagle Creek address answers to Orange County Permitting Services instead, where the code defines turf only as a living grass species and stays silent on a synthetic one. Either way, a 2026 statewide standard sets a floor neither office can undercut on a single-family lot of an acre or less, covered in full at our HB 683 page.

Lake Nona yard types and what we do differently

Yard shapes vary here more than the community's single brand name suggests. Laureate Park's own landscape standards sort residential lots into named types, from a narrow townhome lot to a golf-front estate, and cap how much of each one can be lawn instead of bed or hardscape. Add Eagle Creek and Lake Nona Golf & Country Club's fairway frontage, Storey Park's newer streets, and the ponds that touch nearly every phase, and Lake Nona stops being one yard and turns into six or seven.

What the Laureate Park design guidelines actually say about turf

Laureate Park's Master Association publishes its own landscape standards, last updated in January 2016, and unlike most association documents in the area, this one names artificial turf directly instead of staying silent on it. The rule is narrow: synthetic turf is considered only in a rear yard, decided case by case by the Design Review Board, and only where screening or site conditions support it. Nothing in the document opens a front or side yard to it. Sodded lawns, by contrast, are specified down to the variety, mainly Floritam St. Augustine, Empire Zoysia or Argentine Bahia, and the association's own coverage table caps how much of a lot can be lawn at all, from about a fifth of a townhome's street-facing yard up to half of a mid-size lot's private zone. The alley yard gets its own rule too: lawn there should be minimized, and any lawn that does go in needs at least five feet of width. Eagle Creek runs a separate Architectural Review Committee under its own handbook, so a project there answers to a different board than Laureate Park's. Either way, a permit from Orlando or Orange County settles the legal question; the association still has the final look.

Water, reuse and a watershed divide near the airport

Water in Lake Nona comes from more than one utility, and the management district behind it changes within a few miles too. Homes on the Orlando side of Narcoossee Road typically bill through Orlando Utilities Commission, which waters customers twice weekly while daylight saving time runs and cuts back to once weekly each winter, keeping sprinklers off through the mid-day stretch. Homes east of the road answer to Orange County Utilities instead, on a similar seasonal cadence. Laureate Park layers on a third detail: its own construction standards route irrigation to the City of Orlando's reclaimed-water specification, so part of the community waters its remaining sod with reuse water rather than a potable line. None of that changes what happens to a turf area, since the 2026 standard caps any in-ground system, reclaimed or potable, the moment it would water synthetic grass; the fix is a capped head and a hose rinse either way.

The water management district line runs through the area too. Lake Nona's own drainage flows through the Boggy Creek watershed toward the St. Johns River basin, placing the community under the St. Johns River Water Management District. A few miles southeast, Lake Hart and Lake Mary Jane near Moss Park feed the Kissimmee Chain of Lakes instead, under the South Florida Water Management District. Most addresses never cross that line, but a lot near the Moss Park side of the community can.

Lake Nona itself, Red Lake and the ten-foot rule that follows every pond

The community takes its name from the lake at its center, and water shows up on most streets from there. Red Lake, a 122-acre lake near the airport-side neighborhoods east of Narcoossee, sits close enough to several Eagle Creek and Moss Park-area lots that a backyard survey should note it before anyone measures for turf. Laureate Park and Northlake Park add dozens of smaller stormwater ponds between the houses, and Eagle Creek's golf holes wrap several more. None of that changes the setback: the 2026 turf rule keeps synthetic grass at least ten feet from a natural or built waterbody's ordinary line unless a seawall or bulkhead already stands between the two, and it excludes a pond's littoral shelf outright. Orlando's own landscape code once described a stricter fifty-foot number for artificial turf specifically, a figure the state rule cannot make weaker but also cannot leave tougher on turf than on natural grass covering the same lot. Either way, a lot backing onto open water gets measured before it gets bid.

The sand underneath: soil, drainage and a high water table

Southeast Orange County sits in the flatwoods, and the soil under Lake Nona's newer subdivisions follows the same pattern as the rest of the Boggy Creek watershed: nearly flat, sandy and slow to drain on its own. Series such as Immokalee and Myakka, both mapped across Central Florida's flatwoods by the USDA, describe a sandy profile where groundwater climbs to within a foot or two of grade for stretches of the wet season. A homeowner can pull the exact series for a specific address from the USDA Web Soil Survey, but the practical result holds across the community: a base has to raise the finished grade and drain fast, since the native sand underneath does little on its own once that groundwater rises after a summer storm.

Short-term rentals: a small, tightly zoned market here

Lake Nona reads more like a working community built around medicine and sport than a vacation corridor, and its rental rules follow that pattern. Published guidance on short-term rentals in Orlando restricts a whole-home rental under thirty nights to specific overlay districts and planned developments, and a standard Laureate Park or Northlake Park address sits in ordinary residential zoning outside any of them. East of Narcoossee Road, unincorporated Orange County runs a similar restriction of its own: most residential zoning there carries a thirty-night minimum unless the property holds a Special Use Permit, an approval that is discretionary rather than automatic (a summary of the county rule). None of that rules out guest-proof rental turf for a furnished corporate lease near Medical City, but it does mean the service is a smaller slice of the work here than in a resort corridor such as Kissimmee or Reunion, where nightly rental sits closer to the zoning default.

Two approvals, one packet

A Lake Nona turf project almost always clears two separate desks, and neither substitutes for the other. The permit office, Orlando or Orange County depending on the address, cares about drainage, setbacks and the state's material standard. The community's design board cares about how the yard reads from the street and the alley, and Florida law leaves it real room to do that: an association can still restrict what is visible from the frontage or a neighboring lot, even after the 2026 turf rule took local bans off the table for cities and counties. Since a rear yard behind a six-foot fence usually is not visible from either one, that is often the difference between an easy approval and a longer one. Bringing photos, a product spec sheet and a site plan to the first submittal, the same three items the HOA packet checklist walks through, tends to shorten that conversation rather than stretch it.

Questions people ask

Is my Lake Nona address inside Orlando or unincorporated Orange County?

It depends on which side of Narcoossee Road the parcel sits. West of it, most addresses including Laureate Park and Northlake Park are inside the City of Orlando; east of it, Storey Park, Eagle Creek and the Moss Park area sit in unincorporated Orange County. A parcel search on the county property appraiser's site confirms a specific address.

Does Orlando's turf-specific code reach a home in Eagle Creek?

No. Eagle Creek sits east of Narcoossee Road in unincorporated Orange County, where the county's own code defines turf only as a living grass species. Orlando's landscape-code section on artificial turf only applies inside the city's own limits.

Can artificial turf go in a Laureate Park front yard?

Not under the community's current landscape standards. The document only considers synthetic turf for a rear yard, decided case by case by the Design Review Board, and does not open a front or side yard to it.

What should you look for in the best artificial turf installer near Lake Nona?

Ask for the base depth and material in writing, the product's face weight and infill type, and how the crew plans to work around an alley-lot access point or a pond setback. A written HOA packet, not just a low price, is usually the better sign.

Does the ten-foot pond setback still apply on a golf-front lot in Eagle Creek?

Yes. The state standard measures the setback from the water's ordinary line regardless of whether a golf course or a fence sits behind it, so a green or a lawn on a fairway-front lot still has to clear that buffer unless a seawall already separates the two.
